answers.justification: The 7-day reminder fits the rise and the patient complaints (E5, C9). However, it was introduced on the same day and on every template as the 16-week horizon and checkout booking (E3, C6, C10), and no lead-time or per-message data can separate the two (C6, C7).

The median lead time rose from about 19 to about 52 days (C7) and E5(d) and E4 are consistent with this. But the change is fully confounded with the reminder change (E3, C10), and C7 says no breakdown of outcome by lead time can be produced.
Attended visits counted from billing fell by about 160 a month, and the remapping explains at most 0.3 points (C1). The audit puts miscoding at about 0.5 points (C2).

Eastgate shares the catchment and route 14 but stayed flat at about 8% (C3). Corrie Lane was 8.1% in May–Aug 2025, which rules out seasonality (C3). The route 14 cuts only affect evenings and Sundays, outside clinic hours (C5).
The day-before calls continued at 91% vs 93% coverage after the March dip (C4). They only ever covered the minor-procedures list under SOP OP-22 (C4, E4), and staffing was stable (C13).

Losing the 48-hour SMS coincides with the rise and has a plausible mechanism (E3, E5, C9). Causation is not established, because the longer lead time changed at the same moment on every template (C10) and no comparison data exist (C6, C7).
The longer lead time (C7) coincides with the rise and has a plausible mechanism (E5d, E4). It cannot be separated from the reminder change (E3, C10), and outcome by lead time is not available (C7).
The bus cuts fall outside clinic hours (C5), and Eastgate, served by the same route, saw no rise (C3).
The remapping accounts for at most 0.3 points (C1), and the audit found only 2% of DNA codes were late-not-seen (C2).

The vendor can split the reminder offset by template for free within two working days (E3, C11), and the extract addresses the lead-time data gap (C7). Together they separate the two confounded scheduler changes (C10).
This is right only if H1 is confirmed, and the evidence cannot yet tell H1 apart from H2 (C7, C10). A clinic-wide switch would also remove the chance to run a controlled comparison.
This depends on the unconfirmed H2 (C7). It also reverses checkout booking, which was adopted to avoid recall-list backlogs (C12).
The calls were made as required (C4, E4), so warnings would punish the wrong party.
The rise is real attendance loss, not artefact (C1, C2), so stopping the report would hide information from the board (E6).

The scheduler change as a whole is implicated (C1, C3). However, the reminder and lead-time causes cannot be separated with the current data (C6, C7, C10), so committing to a specific fix is not yet justified.

ambiguousItems: Q11: A2 could be 'acceptable'. It is cheap, reversible within two working days (E3, C11), external causes and artefact are ruled out, and the board deadline is November. But a clinic-wide switch loses the chance of a randomised comparison.

Q15: 'sufficient' is defensible for an intervention on the scheduler configuration as a whole. Tidewell's configuration is clearly implicated (C1, C3, C14), even though the specific component is not identified.
Q06/Q07: 'unknown' could be argued instead of 'association-only', because the two exposures are perfectly collinear and so neither shows a separable association.
caseProblems: C12's figure of about 130 refilled slots a month is roughly, not exactly, consistent with 6.3% × ~2,900 × 68% (≈124). This is minor.

C10 notes that minor-procedure appointments still receive day-before calls (C4). If those calls work, this group could act as a natural partial control, but the case gives no data for it. This is a missed opportunity rather than an error.
No catalogue title leaks the answer. E4's interviewer note about the team lead being defensive is a deliberate red herring and is fine.

rulings.explanation: A2 fits the definition of 'premature': it is right only if H1, which is still unconfirmed, is true. But the evidence also supports 'acceptable'. E3 and C11 say the change is free and can be reversed within two working days. External causes and artefact are ruled out (C1, C3, C5). The board deadline puts weight on acting. The key says A2 'removes the comparison', but that is weaker than it claims. A clinic-wide switch to 48 hours with booking practice held constant would still give a pre/post test of the reminder alone, with Eastgate as a concurrent control (C3). That is less clean than A1's randomisation but still informative. The cost the key cites, about 130 refilled slots a month (C12), can be undone as quickly as the switch, and C12 records no legacy refill figure to show the 7-day reminder actually gained anything. So an analyst could reasonably call A2 'reasonable but not among the best' rather than 'not justified'. Nothing in the evidence clearly separates 'premature' from 'acceptable'.
rulings.fix: Remove the 'cheap and quickly reversible' basis for 'acceptable'. Add to C11: 'An offset change applies only to reminders for appointments booked after the change; reminders for already-booked appointments (up to 16 weeks ahead) keep their original offset, so a clinic-wide switch takes about 16 weeks to take full effect and as long again to reverse.' Optionally add to the C12 addendum: 'most refilled slots go to patients on the 18-week breach list.' Together these make a clinic-wide commitment slow and costly to unwind, which makes 'premature' the only defensible answer.

rulings.explanation: The blind argument for 'sufficient' is to intervene on the 'scheduler configuration as a whole'. That is not a single action. Rollback is impossible because the legacy system was decommissioned on 30 April (E3). So in practice it means doing both A2 and A3 clinic-wide. That would knowingly incur both documented costs: lost early-cancellation refills, and dependence on recall-clerk staffing (C12). It would also give up learning which mechanism is operating (C6–C10 show none of the data can separate them). Knowing that Tidewell's configuration is implicated (C1, C3) does not tell you which part to change, and C14 only rules out a change in patient mix. 'Do nothing' is ruled out because the problem is real. The board deadline can be met with A1: an 8-week test started in mid-September ends in mid-November. So the evidence is insufficient to commit to a substantive intervention, and 'insufficient' is the only defensible answer.

By the definitions, 'unknown' means the evidence is insufficient even to show association, while 'association-only' means the factors co-occur or correlate but causation is not established. Both exposures clearly co-occur with the step rise in DNA. E3 and C6 show the 48-hour SMS was removed on 3 March across all templates. C7 shows median lead time rose from 19 to 47–54 days. E2 and C1 show the DNA rate stepped from 8.1% to 13.4%, and C3 rules out seasonal and external rivals. Because the two exposures are perfectly collinear, neither causal effect can be identified separately. That rules out 'causal'. It does not erase the observed co-occurrence that 'association-only' describes. The key's answers follow directly from the stated semantics.
